newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Most African oil refineries seen unprofitable.
newsitem.headline: Most African oil refineries seen unprofitable.

text.p: More than half of Africa's oil refineries could not be made profitable under any circumstances, said Eric Daffern, group leader of the World Bank oil and gas division.
He told the Africa Oil 1996 conference that modern oil refineries had to be large, fuel efficient, have conversion facilities, operate near capacity and avoid overstaffing.
"Most African refineries fail on all points," Daffern said. Most had been designed before 1973 "and more than half of the refineries in Africa cannot be made profitable whatever you do."
Pricing could be fixed so that they could show a profit but they would not be naturally profitable.
The few exceptions were the refineries in South Africa, he said adding that Nigerian refineries could also be profitable.
Refineries in Ghana, Kenya and Ivory Coast could break even on a cost basis if past investments were not taken into account.
"The rest are too small and cannot be profitable," Daffern said, adding that their combined losses could be more than $500 million a year.

He said most African markets were too small to allow for real competition. This meant that any liberalisation of oil markets would have to be carefully introduced and attention should rather be paid to making the market more competitive.
Daffern said that most African countries still controlled imports, margins and prices "and most do it badly" by not increasing prices as and when they were needed.
Africa remained under-explored and provided vast new opportunities for investors, he said.
But it was unlikely that these opportunites would be taken up unless African countries provided better investment incentives and a more stable operating environment.
Fiscal terms, which he described as "pretty miserable by and large" would have to be improved, legal systems updated and commercial services strengthened.

Some countries insisted that their national oil companies have too large a slice of any new project and further dampened investor enthusiasm by demanding excessive terms which their prospects did not warrant.
